audience.programmeDescription: PPLE at the University of Amsterdam is an English-taught interdisciplinary bachelor in politics, psychology, law and economics. Students complete a shared core, four integrative seminars, one disciplinary major, electives and an interdisciplinary thesis. This example uses the Politics major.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can combine substantial politics, social psychology, law, economics and research methods. Its options prioritise a broad four-field response, behavioural public policy and empirical evaluation, or law, justice and economic governance. PPLE provides a prescribed interdisciplinary sequence and required thesis; the course relationships shown are partial.

componentNotes.y1-01: The first year consists of ten compulsory 6-EC courses. Completing all 60 EC meets the first-year continuation threshold of 54 EC. What You Don’t Learn in School is an additional non-credit requirement in Years 1 and 2.
componentNotes.y2-01: Law and Behaviour requires the first-year Law, Justice and Morality course.
componentNotes.y2-02: Economics for a Changing World II requires Economics for a Changing World I.
componentNotes.y2-04: Politics, Power and Governance II requires the first-year course. Its content centres on European integration, EU institutions and contemporary crises.
componentNotes.y2-06: The Politics major requires Politics, Power and Governance I. The listed Politics courses form one major; courses from the other three majors are not added.
componentNotes.y2-09: The methods course develops quantitative political analysis and qualitative inquiry. Prior Introduction to Statistical Analysis is recommended and is completed in Year 1.
componentNotes.y3-04: Psychology and Society II requires Psychology and Society I. The course examines cultural and cross-cultural psychology.
componentNotes.y3-05: Research Lab develops an interdisciplinary research proposal and offers methodological tutorial tracks. It is a separate compulsory course from the thesis; prior research-methods study is recommended.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The 12-EC thesis is an individual interdisciplinary research report, with an oral defence, in the second semester of Year 3. Entry requires 120 EC from academic core or major courses before that semester; electives do not count. Completing Years 1 and 2 and the first-semester major courses meets this threshold.
componentNotes.y3-open: Twelve EC remain for electives, normally in the first semester of Year 3. Courses outside the designated PPLE electives require Examinations Board approval. An approved 6- or 12-EC internship may use this space; no internship or particular elective is assumed.

cellNotes.text: The first year consists of ten compulsory 6-EC courses. Completing all 60 EC meets the first-year continuation threshold of 54 EC. What You Don’t Learn in School is an additional non-credit requirement in Years 1 and 2.
Law and Behaviour requires the first-year Law, Justice and Morality course.
Economics for a Changing World II requires Economics for a Changing World I.
Politics, Power and Governance II requires the first-year course. Its content centres on European integration, EU institutions and contemporary crises.
The Politics major requires Politics, Power and Governance I. The listed Politics courses form one major; courses from the other three majors are not added.
The methods course develops quantitative political analysis and qualitative inquiry. Prior Introduction to Statistical Analysis is recommended and is completed in Year 1.
Psychology and Society II requires Psychology and Society I. The course examines cultural and cross-cultural psychology.

Research Lab develops an interdisciplinary research proposal and offers methodological tutorial tracks. It is a separate compulsory course from the thesis; prior research-methods study is recommended.

The 12-EC thesis is an individual interdisciplinary research report, with an oral defence, in the second semester of Year 3. Entry requires 120 EC from academic core or major courses before that semester; electives do not count. Completing Years 1 and 2 and the first-semester major courses meets this threshold.

Twelve EC remain for electives, normally in the first semester of Year 3. Courses outside the designated PPLE electives require Examinations Board approval. An approved 6- or 12-EC internship may use this space; no internship or particular elective is assumed.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.text: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.text: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.

BENECON212.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
BENECON212.text: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.text: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

BENECON314.name: Behavioral Economics
BENECON314.text: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.
